exercises.objective: Distinguish model-based, model-free, and policy-search RL by what each learns from data.
exercises.prompt: For each of model-based RL, model-free RL, and policy search, state precisely what is learned from the data $\mathcal{D}=\{(s,a,r,s')\}$.
hints: Model-based RL learns $\hat P(s'\mid s,a)$ and $\hat R(s,a)$, an explicit model of the environment, then plans (RL-02's value/Q-iteration) against that learned model.
Model-free RL learns $V^*(s)$ or $Q^*(s,a)$ directly (RL-03's TD/Q-learning), skipping the model entirely.

Policy search learns (or directly estimates the gradient of) the policy $\pi_\theta$ itself (RL-04), or uses black-box/evolutionary search on $\theta$, without necessarily learning any value function at all.

exercises.objective: Compute the optimistic Q-value initialization from R_max and the discount factor.
exercises.prompt: For $R_\text{max}=10$ and $\gamma=0.9$, compute the optimistic initialization $Q(s,a)=R_\text{max}/(1-\gamma)$. Enter a decimal.
hints: $Q(s,a)=100$: the maximum possible discounted return if you received $R_\text{max}$ every single step forever, an intentionally optimistic (usually far too large in practice, per the source's own note) starting value.

exercises.objective: Explain precisely how Q(s,a) + beta*sigma(s,a) matches OPT-06's UCB1 formula structurally.
exercises.prompt: Explain the structural correspondence between UCB-style Q-value exploration, $Q(s,a)+\beta\sigma(s,a)$, and OPT-06's UCB1 bandit formula, term by term.
hints: OPT-06's UCB1 chooses the arm maximizing $\mu_a+\beta\sqrt{2\ln n/n_a}$: a point estimate $\mu_a$ plus a confidence-bound bonus that's large for under-visited arms and shrinks as $n_a$ grows.

$Q(s,a)$ plays exactly the role of $\mu_a$ (a current point estimate of value), and $\sigma(s,a)$ plays exactly the role of the confidence bound (large when $(s,a)$ is poorly-estimated/rarely-visited, shrinking with more visits).

Both formulas implement the identical 'optimism in the face of uncertainty' principle: add a bonus proportional to how uncertain the current estimate is, so uncertain options get tried, and the bonus naturally fades as uncertainty is resolved by experience; RL-05's version simply applies this bandit-derived idea to sequential-decision Q-values instead of single-shot bandit arms.

exercises.objective: Explain why R-max's strictly-optimistic reward mechanism requires no separately-designed exploration bonus.
exercises.prompt: Explain why planning (via RL-02's value/Q-iteration) against $R_\text{R-max}$ automatically produces an exploring policy, with no separate exploration term added to the objective.
hints: Every state-action pair visited fewer than $m$ times is assigned reward $R_\text{max}$ (the theoretical maximum), regardless of what its true reward actually is.

Value/Q-iteration, run against this optimistic reward function, will therefore compute a very high value for any path that leads toward unvisited/under-visited $(s,a)$ pairs, since reaching them looks (falsely, but usefully) like reaching maximum reward.

The resulting 'optimal' policy under $R_\text{R-max}$ is therefore automatically driven to seek out under-explored regions of the state-action space, purely as a side effect of ordinary reward-maximizing planning; once $(s,a)$ becomes known ($c(s,a)\geq m$), its true estimated reward replaces the optimistic placeholder, and the optimism naturally fades exactly where it's no longer needed.
